# brickie

> brickie measures a Rust workspace (module dependency edges, per-function complexity) and checks
> it against rules the maintainers wrote in `brickie.toml`; the rules are the project's
> architecture. This static guide is for coding agents in a repository that uses brickie.

## Workflow

1. `brickie measure` reads the code (cargo metadata, rust-analyzer, tree-sitter) and writes
   `.brickie/cache.json` next to `brickie.toml`. It is slow: run it once per round of edits.
2. `brickie check` reads the cache and rules, prints diagnostics, and exits non-zero on a
   finding. It is fast and never runs rust-analyzer unless you pass `--measure`. It
   checks structure (edges, complexity), not runtime behaviour: pair it with the project's own
   tests.
3. Fix the code each diagnostic points at.
4. Repeat until the exit code is 0.

- The gate, in one command: `brickie check --measure --format short`. `--measure` re-measures
  first when the cache is missing or older than the code. `--format short` prints one line per
  finding: `error[deps/deny] 3fa9c1d2 src/a.rs:42:17: message`; use the default text format to
  see the rule, help and notes of a finding you need to fix.
- A cache older than the code is an error (`stale/*`, exit 1), never a pass: after any code
  change re-measure before trusting `check`. Config edits never need a re-measure.
- `--measure` needs `rust-analyzer` on `PATH`; when the measure fails, `check` exits 2 and
  prints the reason.
- `brickie check --format json` prints `{summary, diagnostics}`; each finding has `id`, `code`,
  `brick_level`, `message`, `span`, `spans`, `rule`, `help`, `notes`, `bricks`, `edges`. Read the text form, loop over the JSON.
- `brickie check --brick PATH` (repeatable; path from the root such as `web/api`, includes
  descendants) shows only findings owned by that brick: the source brick of `deps/*` edges, all
  members of a `deps/cycle`, the defining brick of `interface/*`, the
  function's brick of `complexity/*`. Findings with no owner always show. The whole workspace is
  still checked; the footer `outside scope: N errors` counts what is hidden, and the
  exit code uses the shown findings only.
- While coding brick X: `brickie check --brick X`. A scoped check can exit 0 while errors remain
  outside the scope: before reporting done, run the full gate with no `--brick`. JSON adds an
  `outside_scope` object when `--brick` is used.
- `brickie interface <brick-path> [--json]` (for example `root/web/api`) prints the brick's
  declared interface: every item outside code can name, with signature, first doc paragraph,
  definition, and uses (grouped by using brick, file:line:col per site; `[test]` marks test code);
  unused items are marked `UNUSED`. Read it before using or changing a brick from outside.
  `--from <brick-path>` instead lists every reference site from that brick into this one, by used
  item. JSON lists every site; text shows five per using brick.
- `brickie serve` is a web viewer for humans; you do not need it.
- Every command accepts `--config path/to/brickie.toml` (default `./brickie.toml`).

Exit codes of `brickie check`: 0 clean, 1 at least one finding (a stale cache included), 2
configuration, cache or argument problem (for example no cache: run `brickie measure`). `brickie interface` exits 2 on
any error; `brickie design` exits 3 on a stale base and 4 when `publish` is blocked.

## Features and targets

`measure` always indexes with all cargo features on, for the host target, plus one run per
target in `[measure] additional_targets` of the root `brickie.toml`; edges of all runs are
merged. Principles to follow when writing code:

- P1: features are additive; the code builds with any combination (`--all-features` must work).
- P2: a feature selects an optional capability; `cfg(target_*)` selects the platform.
- P3: a feature adds an optional dependency or adapter; it does not change existing API.
- P4: conditional code lives at the edges: adapters and the composition root.

After `measure`, a line `hint: code under cfg(target_arch = "wasm32") is not measured; add
"wasm32-unknown-unknown" to [measure] additional_targets` means that code has no edges in the
cache, so a rule it uses may look unused. Do not add the target yourself; report the hint to the
reviewer. If `measure` fails with "rust-analyzer scip failed for target ..." and "if features are
mutually exclusive, make them additive", fix the code so a build with all features works, or
report that the target is not installed (`rustup target add <target>`).

## Hard constraints

- Never edit `brickie.toml` (or files it includes) to make `check` pass;
  they are the project's decisions. Change the design only when the human asked for a design
  change, and only with `brickie design` (see "Editing the design"), never by hand. Never use
  `brickie design` to make a finding go away (adding an allow rule, raising or removing a limit,
  exporting a child, removing a deny rule): report the finding instead.
- Every finding is an error and there is no way to accept one: only a human relaxes the design
  (a rule or limit). If a finding looks wrong or a rule too strict, stop and report it with the
  finding id.
- Do not split a function mechanically to get under a complexity limit (forwarding helpers, one
  statement per function). Reduce real complexity: early returns, a table instead of a branch
  chain, a struct instead of many parameters, a clearer decomposition.
- Do not move code or add re-exports to hide a dependency from the checker; the edge is measured
  where the code references the other module.

## Editing the design

The design has two trees. The published tree is the real `brickie.toml` files: `brickie check`
and the gate read only it. The draft (`.brickie/draft/`, one at a time) is where every
`brickie design` edit goes; the first edit creates it, forked from the published head. The
published tree changes only by `brickie design publish`, which copies the draft into the real
files once the code matches the draft's structure. Versions are numbered once for both trees
(`v15`), each tagged with its track (`draft` or `published`); `.brickie/history/` keeps the last
200 (who, when, note, ops, semantic diff). Your edits are recorded as `agent`, the viewer's as
`human`, and a hand edit of the published files as `external`. Never edit the config files by
hand; use `brickie design`.

### Draft workflow

1. `brickie design show`: with a draft it prints `design draft v42 from published v37 ...`,
   without one `design published v37 ...`. Use the version it prints as `--base`.
2. Edit the draft (`apply` or the write commands). The draft is free-style: only config syntax
   and self-consistency are checked (`design/invalid`), never the code. Its `show` todo lists
   only config items such as `design/no-reason`.
3. `brickie design publish --dry-run --base N` prints the refactor checklist: every blocking
   item (`config/unassigned`, `config/overlap`, `config/member-outside-parent`, `design/planned`,
   a stale or missing cache) with its draft file and member selector, plus the dependency
   findings of the draft as not blocking.
4. Refactor the code until the checklist is empty, running `brickie measure` after each change.
   Code written for bricks that exist only in the draft shows as `bricks/unmapped` in
   `brickie check` until the publish; that is expected. `--scaffold` is allowed and creates the
   code of draft bricks.
5. `brickie design publish --base N` writes the draft as ONE published version and removes the
   draft. It exits 4 (`design/blocked`) while any item remains and publishes nothing; there is
   no partial publish. Dependency and rule findings (deny, private, cycles, limits, unused,
   no-reason) never block: `brickie check` reports them after the publish.

If the published tree moved since the fork (a hand edit, an undo of a published version),
`publish` exits 3 (`design/stale`) and lists those versions: run
`brickie design rebase --base N` (N: the draft head) to replay the draft's ops onto the new
published head; an op that clashes fails and nothing is written (undo that draft version, or
discard). `brickie design discard --base N` drops the draft; the history keeps a marker.

Concurrency contract (a human may edit at the same time):

- Run `brickie design show` at the start of every design task and use the base it prints (the
  draft head, or the published head when there is no draft yet); never
  reuse a base you remember. Any read or write may record a pending hand edit as an `external`
  version first, so the head can move under you (`--dry-run` prints the head it ran on).
- Every write takes `--base N` (or set `BRICKIE_BASE`) and `--note "why"`, which the human reads
  in the log. When the design has moved on, nothing is
  written and the command exits 3:

  ```
  error[design/stale]: design is at v15 (by human, 12s ago), your edit was based on v13. Nothing was written.
  Changes since v13:
    v14 by agent:
      + brickie.toml: brick store
  Re-read with `brickie design show`, then retry with --base 15.
  ```

  Re-read (`show`, or `show --since N`), check the changes still allow your edit, and retry once
  on the new base. If it is stale again, or a human's version changed what you were editing, stop
  and ask the human; stop too when your edit contradicts a human's note. An unknown base (newer
  than the head, or older than the kept history) also gives exit 3.
- After your first write, `show` starts with a `since your last version (agent):` header listing
  the human and external versions since then (author, note, diff lines); read them before you
  edit. It is empty until you have written once, and when there is nothing new.
- `undo [V]` reverts the file changes of version V (default: the working head) as a new version
  of V's track, comments included; `--base` is the head of that track. Undoing a draft version
  changes the draft; undoing a published version (such as a publish) restores the published
  bytes. It refuses when a later version changed the same file and was not undone. Never undo
  a human's or an external version (the CLI refuses); ask the human. After a nested
  `brickie.toml` was deleted, `show` warns and `undo` restores it. `undo` never removes
  scaffolded code.

- `show` prints `design draft v16 from published v15 <hash>` (or `design published v15 <hash>`)
  and the tree: each level
  with its file, bricks (kind, members, tags, children), rules `from -> to (scope)
  allow|deny "reason"` and limits, then a `todo` list. `--since N` prints only the
  versions after N, each with its author, note and diff lines. `--in P` prints only the level
  owned by composite P and its subtree (use it on a large design).
- A write prints `ok: draft v16` (`ok: draft v16 from published v15` when it started the draft,
  `... (no change)` when nothing changed), lists the design files
  and any code it created, then one `note: ...` line per fact worth knowing. A write that would leave the design invalid writes nothing (`design/invalid`).
- Bricks are named by path from the root (`web/api`, `root/web/api` is the same); a level by the
  composite brick that owns it (`--in web`; default: the root level). Never use indices.
- Prefer one `apply` per task: `brickie design apply --base N --note "why"` reads one op per
  stdin line and writes them all as ONE version, so the human sees one toast and has one Undo.
  A line is a write command without the `brickie design` prefix and without `--base`, `--note`
  or `--dry-run`; blank lines and lines whose first character is `#` are ignored (a `#` elsewhere
  is part of the value); quote values with spaces (`"..."` or `'...'`):

  ```
  brickie design apply --base 15 --note "add store" <<'EOF'
  brick add store --kind crate --desc "data access"
  rule add web store allow --reason "web reads data"
  EOF
  ```

  A bad line stops everything: the error names the line number and nothing is written. Names
  in a line resolve against the design as it is now, so a line cannot refer to a brick an
  earlier line adds, except by `brick add --in` or in a rule's `FROM`/`TO`.
- `--dry-run` (on `apply` and on every write command) checks the base, applies and validates
  everything in memory, prints the diff, the todos the change adds and the notes, and writes
  nothing (no version, no code). With `--scaffold` it also lists the code it would create.
  Use it before a large `apply`.

Commands (each write also takes `--base N`, `--note` and `--dry-run`; `undo`, `rebase` and
`discard` take `--base` only; `--scaffold` is only on `brick add` and `apply`):

```
brickie design show [--since N] [--in P] [--format json]
brickie design log | diff A [B] | undo [V]
brickie design apply [--scaffold]   (ops on stdin, one per line)
brickie design publish --base N [--dry-run] [--note W] | rebase --base N | discard --base N
brickie design brick add NAME [--in P] [--kind crate|module|group] [--members a,b] [--tags a,b] [--desc D] [--path DIR] [--scaffold]
brickie design brick set PATH [--members] [--tags] [--desc] [--path]   (empty --desc/--path removes)
brickie design brick rename PATH NEW | move PATH --into P|root | rm PATH
brickie design brick group NAME CHILD... | ungroup PATH
brickie design rule add FROM TO allow|deny [--via A,B] [--kind K]... [--scope S] [--reason R] [--in P]
brickie design rule set FROM TO [--kind K]... [--scope S] [--action A] [--via A,B] [--reason R] [--in P]
brickie design rule rm FROM TO [--kind K]... [--scope S] [--in P]
brickie design export set PATH | rm PATH
brickie design limit add|set [BRICKS] [--cognitive N] [--cyclomatic N] [--nesting N] [--paths N] [--params N] [--lines N] [--scope S] [--in P]
brickie design limit rm [BRICKS] [--in P]
brickie design include add|rm FILE [--in P]
```

- A rule is named by `from`, `to`, its kinds and scope (scope `prod` when not written). `rule set`
  and `rule rm` search the level file and the files it includes; with several rules `FROM -> TO`
  add `--kind` / `--scope` to pick one. `rule set` changes only the fields given (an empty
  `--reason` or `--via` removes it); to change kinds or scope, remove the rule and add a new one.
- `--via A,B` limits a rule to edges that enter the `to` composite through its exported children
  A or B (see "Rules"); the rule is still named by `from`, `to`, kinds and scope. Renaming such a
  child rewrites the `via` of the rules that name it; removing, moving or unexporting it, or
  ungrouping the composite, fails with `design/invalid` while a `via` would dangle.
- A limit is named by its `bricks` selector (default `*`); in `limit set` a metric of `0` removes
  it.
- `brick add --kind crate` with no members defaults them to `path:crates/<name>/`
  (`path:<name>/` in a nested file); `--kind group` makes a composite in its own folder
  `<name>/` next to its parent file, with a new `brickie.toml`. Pass `--path` or `--members` to
  choose. `brick set NAME --path P` makes a module composite and creates
  `P/brickie.toml` when it is absent. brickie writes no source code unless asked: the brick
  shows as a `planned` todo until you write the code. `--scaffold` (on `brick add`, or on `apply`
  for every line; not allowed inside a line) also creates the missing code (folder, crate
  `Cargo.toml` and `src/lib.rs` plus a workspace member, or a module file plus `pub mod` in the
  crate root; the write lists what it created); existing files are never overwritten. The
  design files of a group and of `set --path` are always created.
- `rule add` (also as an `apply` line) prints `note: rule a -> b allow changes nothing: already
  allowed by brickie.toml:12` when the new rule changes no edge of its level (also for an allow
  from an independent brick to a normal one, which never applies).
  It is a note, not an error: the rule is written. No note when the level is created in the
  same `apply`.
- A rule's `scope` is `prod` unless set: edges from test code need `rule add ... --scope test|all`.
- `brick group NAME CHILD...` makes composite NAME next to the children and moves them in;
  `ungroup` lifts the children, their rules and limits back up (the child file stays on disk).
  `brick move` rebases `path:` members; it moves no code.
- `brick rename` also renames the brick in the rules, limit selectors and exports of its file.
- After code changes run `brickie measure`, then `brickie design publish --dry-run` (while a draft
  exists) or `brickie design show` (the todo list), and `brickie check`.
- `--format json`: `show` also has `since_agent: [version...]` when there are versions after your
  last one; `--dry-run` prints `{dry_run, diff, new_todo, scaffold, notes}`; a write prints its version, plus `notes: [text]` when there are notes. `show` prints `{v, track, forked_from, hash, by, at, root: {path, file, bricks: [{name, kind,
  members, tags, desc, todo, children}], exports, rules: [{file, from, to, via,
  kinds, scope, action, reason, todo}], limits: [{file, bricks, metrics, scope}]}, todo:
  [{kind, text}]}`; `log` a list of versions `{v, track, forked_from, reverts, hash, prev, by, at, note,
  ops, diff, files, removed}`; a write prints its version; `publish --dry-run` prints
  `{dry_run, draft, forked_from, ready, blocking: [{code, message, file, brick, member,
  module}], info: [text]}`.

The todo list of the published design (`kind`): `planned` a brick with no measured module
(`design/planned`), `unused` an allow rule between named bricks no measured edge uses
(it decides no edge yet), `reason` a rule without a reason (`design/no-reason`), `config` a partition
error or a cache problem. A draft's todo list has `reason` items only; what its code lacks is
the `publish --dry-run` checklist.

## Reading a diagnostic

```
error[deps/deny]: `engine` depends on `backends`
  --> src/engine/mixer.rs:42:17
   |
42 |         let io = backends::Alsa::open();
   |                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ `backends::Alsa`
   = rule: rule[0] "core must not use adapter" (brickie.toml:21)
   = help: depend on the port trait and receive the implementation from the assembly
   = note: modules: engine::mixer -> backends::alsa (uses, prod)
```

- Header: `error`, the code in brackets, a message. Every finding fails `check`.
- `-->` is the primary location `file:line:col`; extra locations follow ("and N more").
- `rule` names the configured rule that fired and where it is; it holds the maintainers' reason.
- `help` is the suggested fix; `note` adds context (for example the full cycle path).
- Every finding has a stable 8-hex `id` (in JSON).
- The last line summarises: `error: 3 errors` (or `ok: 0 errors`).

Vocabulary:

- A brick is a named group of crates or modules from `[[brick]]`. An edge is a reference from a
  module in one brick to an item in a module of another.
- Edge kinds (one per reference site): `uses` (call, type, constant), `implements`
  (`impl Trait for X` where the trait lives elsewhere), `reexports` (a `use` with any `pub`
  visibility; private `use` leaves count as `uses`).
- The edge target is always the module that DEFINES the item, even when reached through a
  re-export; a finding's note shows `written <path as written> -> defined in <module>`.
- Scope is `test` for code under a package's own `tests/` or `benches/` directory and for items
  gated by `#[cfg(test)]` or `#[cfg(all(test, ..))]` (a `mod x;` declared that way included);
  everything else is `prod`, also `any(test, ..)`, `not(test)`, `cfg_attr` and `feature = ".."`
  gates. Test edges are checked like prod edges. Edges inside one brick, or touching a module in no brick, are ignored.
- Nested bricks: a brick with `path = "<dir>"` is a composite; its children, rules and `exports`
  are in `<dir>/brickie.toml`. A finding's JSON `brick_level` (`root`, `root/web`) is the tree
  level it is reported at; its brick names are children of that level and `rule` points at the
  config file owning the rule. An edge is checked against the rules of the lowest common ancestor
  of its two bricks (`web/ui` to `core` is checked as `web -> core` in the root file).

## Diagnostic codes and how to fix them

### deps/deny

An edge between sibling bricks is not allowed: a `[[rule]]` with `action = "deny"` decides it
(`rule` names it), or no rule allows it, or it leaves an independent brick (see "Rules"). Remove
the dependency: depend on a
trait, type or function in a brick you may use, and have the assembling brick pass the concrete
implementation in. If the code is test-only, use `#[cfg(test)]` or move it under `tests/` (many
rules apply only to `prod`). If the dependency is truly intended, report it for a human reviewer;
do not edit the rule.

### deps/private

The edge reaches into a composite brick through a child not listed in its `exports` (the message
names the composite and the hidden child; `rule` is the composite's config file). Use what the
composite exports. Re-exporting the item through an exported child does not help: the edge points
at the defining module. If the child should be visible, report it; the maintainers may add it to
`exports`.

### deps/cycle

Two or more bricks depend on each other, directly or through others; the note shows the cycle.
Break it: move the shared type into a trait or type owned by the lower brick, or invert one
dependency so the lower brick receives what it needs from the higher one (parameter, trait object,
callback). Do not merge bricks in `brickie.toml`. Cycles are found per level, among the children
of one composite (`brick_level` says which).

### complexity/cognitive, complexity/cyclomatic, complexity/nesting, complexity/paths, complexity/params, complexity/lines

One finding per function and metric above the limit of a `[[complexity]]` rule (inclusive:
"limit 15" fails at 16). The message gives the value and the limit. Metrics:

- `cognitive`: how hard the function is to read. `+1 + nesting` per `if`, `match` (once, not per
  arm), `for`, `while`, `loop`, `let ... else`; `+1` per `else`; `+1` per sequence of like `&&` /
  `||`; `+1` per labeled `break`/`continue` and per direct recursive call. `?` is free. Closures
  add nesting but no cost themselves (as in SonarSource). Macro bodies (token trees such as
  `println!(..)`, `vec![..]`, `view! {..}`) are not parsed, so branching inside them is not
  measured. Fix:
  guard clauses and early `return`/`continue`, `?` instead of nested matches, extract a cohesive step.
- `cyclomatic`: `1 + if + loops + (match arms - 1) + let-else + && + || + ?`. Fix: replace long
  chains with a lookup table, data-driven code, or split by responsibility.
- `nesting`: deepest nesting of branches, loops and closures. Fix: invert conditions and return
  early, flatten with `let ... else`, extract the inner body when it is a meaningful unit.
- `paths` (simplified NPath): an estimate of execution paths. An `if` is `then + else` (an absent
  `else` counts 1); a `match` is the sum of its arms, and a `match` of 3 or more constant arms
  counts 1; a loop is `body + 1`; each `?`, `&&` and `||` adds 1. Sequential decisions add; they
  do not multiply as in textbook NPath. Fix: reduce independent branches in one function, separate unrelated decisions into
  functions with a clear contract, use tables for constant `match` arms.
- `params`: parameters other than `self`. Fix: group related parameters into a struct or options
  type that has a meaning in the domain (not a bag of unrelated values).
- `lines`: lines of the function. Fix: split along real responsibilities.

Which limit applies is rule 8 under "Rules". Test-scope functions are checked only when the
rule's `scope` includes tests. Never raise a limit; never add
`#[cfg(test)]` or move code only to change its scope.

### stale/file (error)

A `.rs` file was changed, added or deleted after `brickie measure`, or a workspace crate
(a `[workspace] members` entry of the root `Cargo.toml`) was added or removed (the message says
which), so its data is old. Run `brickie check --measure` (or `brickie measure`, then
`brickie check`). 

### stale/measure (error)

The cache was measured with other features or `additional_targets` than `[measure]` asks for now,
or it was measured in another directory (the project was copied or moved together with its
`.brickie` folder; the message names the old directory). No file is judged then. Run
`brickie check --measure` (or `brickie measure`, then `brickie check`).

### bricks/unmapped (error)

A module belongs to no brick, so none of its edges or functions are checked (usually after adding
a file, module or crate). Unchecked code must not pass. Add it to the `members` of a brick (`brickie design brick set PATH --members ...`)
only when the right brick is obvious from the surrounding code; otherwise ask the reviewer. No
re-measure is needed.

### interface/unused (error)

A leaf brick declares an item (reachable from outside: public API of its crate, or a `pub` /
`pub(crate)` item whose module is visible to another brick) that no code outside the brick and no
test uses (tests anywhere count, including the brick's own). The location is the definition. Fix:
if only the brick needs it, make it private, or remove it if nothing uses it; or add a test that
exercises it. Methods, fields and variants count as uses of their type; `pub use` re-exports are
not uses.

### config/missing, config/invalid, config/unknown-via, config/overlap, config/unassigned, config/member-outside-parent

Configuration errors (exit 2, printed on stderr with the code first; no findings are reported):

- `config/missing`: a brick has `path = "<dir>"` but `<dir>/brickie.toml` does not exist.
- `config/invalid`: a file does not follow the schema: a rule or limit names a brick or tag the
  file lacks, an unknown kind, `exports` names something that is not a brick of that file, or
  `independent = true` is on a brick of a nested file. The message says which.
- `config/unknown-via`: a rule's `via` is empty, its `to` is not a brick name of a composite, or
  it names a child the composite does not export. Fix `via` (or the composite's `exports`).
- `config/overlap`: a module matches members of two bricks of one file.
- `config/unassigned`: a module of a composite is in none of its children (children must
  partition the composite).
- `config/member-outside-parent`: a child's member matches a module outside its composite.
These are brick-structure decisions: report them rather than editing the config to silence them.

A composite owns every module under its path, and a brick of an outer level must not match one
from inside it (that would bypass its `exports`): that is `config/overlap` at the outer level. Remove
that member from the outer brick and make it a child brick of the composite; add it to the
composite's `exports` if outside code uses it. A `path:` member matches a package whose directory
is under it, and a module whose source file is under it, so `path:src/lib.rs` names a crate root.

In a draft these are the blocking items of `brickie design publish --dry-run`: either change
the code to the drawn structure, or change the draft. Give each unassigned module to one of
the composite's bricks (`brick set --members`), make overlapping members distinct, keep child
members inside their composite. `check` lists every partition error at once.

### design/planned, design/no-reason, design/invalid, design/stale, design/no-match, design/exists, design/blocked

The design (see "Editing the design"):

- `design/planned` (todo `planned`, a blocking item of `publish`): a brick has no measured
  module. Create its code as its members say, then `brickie measure`.
- `design/no-reason` (todo `reason`): a rule has no `reason`. Add a one-line reason with
  `brickie design rule set FROM TO --reason "..."`.
- `design/invalid`: the edit would leave a design that does not load (for example a rule naming
  an unknown brick). Nothing was written. Fix the edit, or make the
  related change in the same order the message suggests (for example change the rule first).
- `design/stale` (exit code 3): your `--base` is not the head; nothing was written. Follow the
  concurrency contract in "Editing the design". From `publish`: the published tree moved since
  the draft's fork; run `brickie design rebase --base N`, then publish again.
- `design/blocked` (exit code 4): `publish` refused because the code does not match the draft's
  structure yet; nothing was published. The message lists the items; work through
  `brickie design publish --dry-run --base N` (see "Draft workflow").
- `design/no-match`: no rule or limit matches what you named, or several rules `FROM -> TO` match.
  The message lists the candidates; name an existing one, or add `--kind` and `--scope` to pick
  one. For bricks, check the path with `brickie design show`.
- `design/exists`: `rule add` or `limit add` for an identity that is already there. Change it with
  `rule set` / `limit set`, or remove it first.

## brickie.toml reference

```toml
[[brick]]
name = "engine"                # unique in this file
members = ["my-engine", "my-app::api", "path:crates/engine/"]
                               # package name (all targets) | module prefix (and descendants) |
                               # path:<dir>/ (crates whose manifest, or modules whose file, are under the folder, relative
                               # to this file). Default: none
tags = ["core"]                # optional labels for rule selectors
desc = "Rule evaluation"       # optional one-liner shown in the viewer; no effect on checks
independent = false            # root file only: acts like an external library (see "Rules")

[[brick]]
name = "app"
members = ["my-app"]
tags = ["app"]

[[rule]]
from = "tag:app"               # selector: brick name | tag:<tag> | *
to = "tag:core"
# via = ["api"]                # optional, `to` a composite brick: only edges entering it through
                               # these exported children match (each must be in its `exports`)
kinds = ["uses", "implements"] # uses | implements | reexports; default all
scope = "prod"                 # prod (default) | test | all
action = "allow"               # allow | deny (required)
reason = "app calls into core" # shown in findings; a rule without one is a design todo

[measure]                      # root file only
additional_targets = ["wasm32-unknown-unknown"]
                               # target triples measured besides the host (default none);
                               # all cargo features are always on

[[complexity]]
bricks = "tag:core"            # selector; default *
cognitive = 15                 # any of cognitive, cyclomatic, nesting, paths, params, lines
nesting = 3
scope = "prod"                 # prod (default) | test | all
```

A composite and the keys that need one (shown as text because the child file must exist):

```toml
# brickie.toml
include = ["presets/layered.toml"]   # optional; relative to this file; merged first, recursively
exports = ["api"]              # composite files only: children visible from outside (default
                               # none); each must name a brick of that file
[[brick]]
name = "web"
path = "crates/web"            # composite: children in crates/web/brickie.toml (required);
                               # members default to ["path:crates/web/"]
```

Every `brickie.toml` (root or composite) has the same schema; `include` works in each. Lists
(`brick`, `exports`, `rule`, `complexity`, `additional_targets`) of included files and the
including file are concatenated. An include cycle, a duplicate brick name in a level, a composite
path that leads back to a file already being loaded, and unknown fields are configuration errors
(exit 2). Each target triple is trimmed, non-empty and has only ASCII letters, digits, `-`, `_`
and `.`.

## Rules

Each rule below holds for every level and has one reason.

1. Bricks: a brick is a named group of modules; its members are packages, module prefixes or
   `path:<dir-or-file>` (`path:src/lib.rs` names one crate root). Reason: the architecture is drawn over code that already exists.
2. Membership: at every level each module belongs to exactly one brick. A module that matches
   members of two bricks of one file is `config/overlap`, whatever the members' specificity (a
   package and a module prefix inside it overlap; list the modules explicitly instead). A module in
   no brick is `bricks/unmapped` at the root and `config/unassigned` inside a composite. Reason:
   every edge and function is judged once, by one brick.
3. Levels: a brick with `path = "<dir>"` is a composite whose children are in
   `<dir>/brickie.toml`; names and tags are local to their file. Reason: each team owns its
   folder's design.
4. Edges: every reference is an edge with a kind (`uses`, `implements`, `reexports`) and a scope
   (`prod`, `test`). It is lifted to the lowest level where its ends are sibling bricks and judged
   there only. A cycle among siblings is always `deps/cycle`. Reason: a rule speaks about the
   bricks it can see, and layers do not form cycles.
5. Rules: a `[[rule]]` matches an edge when `from`, `to`, `kinds` and `scope` match. Selector
   specificity is brick 3, tag 2, `*` 1, summed over both sides; the highest wins and deny wins a
   tie. A rule with `via` (exported children of its `to` composite) matches only an edge that
   enters `to` through one of them, never an edge into a leaf, and scores one more on the `to` side;
   the finding names the entered child. An edge no rule matches is denied (`* -> *` allow opens a level). Every forbidden edge is
   `deps/deny`. Reason: the design lists what is allowed; anything new needs a decision.
6. Exports: from outside a composite, an edge may enter it only through a child in its `exports`,
   whatever the rules say; otherwise `deps/private`. Reason: a composite's internals stay private.
7. Independent: a root brick with `independent = true` acts like an external library. `*` never
   matches it, on either side. Edges into it are allowed unless a deny rule naming it by brick or
   tag wins. Edges out of it are denied unless they go to another independent brick and an allow
   rule names both sides; an allow from it to a normal brick never applies. Exports still apply.
   Reason: a library knows nothing of the application that uses it.
8. Complexity: a `[[complexity]]` rule sets limits for the bricks its selector matches; every
   limit is an error. Per function and metric, each level on the function's brick path applies its
   most specific matching rule (an equal selector takes the lower limit); across levels the
   tightest limit wins, so a nested file only tightens. Reason: a nested file cannot hide code
   from a limit set above it.

Severity and exit: every finding is an error and gives exit 1; there is no warning level and
no way to accept a finding or skip a code. Passing means fixing the code or, for a human, relaxing
the design. `--brick` with an unknown brick gives exit 2.
